blind_target.title: Atypical cerebral lateralisation in adults with compensated developmental dyslexia demonstrated using functional transcranial Doppler ultrasound
blind_target.evidence_quote: Theories have proposed that disruption to the typical left hemisphere dominance for language may be a neurobiological correlate of language problems (e.g., Annett, 2002; Bishop, 2013; Crow et al., 1998), and empirical studies of very small samples have supported that view (Illingworth & Bishop, 2009; Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008). However, the present study did not replicate these findings, and we suggest that they are likely to have been false positives.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Theories have proposed that disruption to the typical left hemisphere dominance for language may be a neurobiological correlate of language problems (e.g., Annett, 2002; Bishop, 2013; Crow et al., 1998), and empirical studies of very small samples have supported that view (Illingworth & Bishop, 2009; Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008). However, the present study did not replicate these findings, and we suggest that they are likely to have been false positives.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly identify the earlier finding being re-tested and report its nonreplication.

blind_target.title: A reaching test reveals weak hand preference in specific language impairment and developmental co-ordination disorder

blind_target.authors: Groen, M., Whitehouse, A., Badcock, N., & Bishop, D.
blind_target.title: Does cerebral lateralization develop? A study using functional transcranial Doppler ultrasound assessing lateralization for language production and visuospatial memory
blind_target.evidence_quote: In the second step of analysis, we tested the relationship between language and laterality from the opposite direction, using language measures as predictors, aiming to replicate the effects reported by Groen et al. (2012). We computed Spearman’s correlations between each language measure and the fTCD laterality index in the two replication samples. However, no uncorrected correlation replicated across samples, and no correlation within a sample survived a Holm-Bonferroni correction.

The reference identifies Illingworth and Bishop (2009) as a distinct empirical fTCD study in adults with dyslexia; the only supplied shipped original is Bishop (2005), a separate handedness study.
